Rootograms for count regressions

Author

Maciej Beręsewicz

1 Introduction

A rootogram (Tukey, 1977; Kleiber & Zeileis, 2016) is a graphical goodness-of-fit display for count models. For each observed count \(k\) it compares

  • the observed frequency \(n_k = \#\{i : y_i = k\}\),
  • the expected frequency under the fitted model \(\hat n_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat P(Y_i = k \mid \mathbf{x}_i;\hat{\boldsymbol\theta})\).

In a hanging rootogram the bar of height \(\sqrt{n_k}\) hangs from the curve \(\sqrt{\hat n_k}\), so its bottom sits at \(\sqrt{\hat n_k} - \sqrt{n_k}\). The square-root scale stretches the tails so small frequencies are still visible. Reading the picture is easy:

  • bar bottom on the zero line → model fits this count perfectly,
  • bar bottom below zero → model under-predicts that count (the data have more cases than expected),
  • bar bottom above zero → model over-predicts.

In R rootograms are available via the topmodels package (successor to countreg) and accept any fitted count model (glm, glm.nb, hurdle, zeroinfl, …). In Python there is no mainstream package that does this, so we write a small helper that reproduces what topmodels::rootogram shows.

2 Setup

  • R
  • Python
## install.packages("topmodels", repos = "https://R-Forge.R-project.org")
#remotes::install_svn("svn://R-Forge.R-project.org/svnroot/topmodels/pkg/topmodels")

library(topmodels)
library(MASS)
library(here)
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from scipy.stats import poisson, nbinom
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

3 Data

We reuse the Polish Job Vacancy Survey (vacancies per company), the same dataset as in lecture 9.

  • R
  • Python
df <- read.csv(here("data/polish-jvs.csv"),
               colClasses = c("character", "factor", rep("character", 4), "numeric"))
df$size   <- factor(df$size,   levels = c("Large", "Medium", "Small"))
df$public <- factor(df$public)
df$nace   <- factor(df$nace)
from pathlib import Path
csv_path = Path("data/polish-jvs.csv")
if not csv_path.exists():
    csv_path = Path("../../data/polish-jvs.csv")

df = pd.read_csv(csv_path,
                 dtype={"id": np.int64, "woj": str, "public": str,
                        "size": str, "nace_division": str, "nace": str})
df["size"] = pd.Categorical(df["size"], categories=["Large", "Medium", "Small"])

4 Fit Poisson and Negative Binomial models

  • R
  • Python
pois <- glm(vacancies ~ size + public + nace, data = df,
            family = poisson(link = "log"))
nb2  <- MASS::glm.nb(vacancies ~ size + public + nace, data = df)
pois = smf.glm("vacancies ~ C(size) + C(public) + C(nace)", data=df,
               family=sm.families.Poisson()).fit()

# Joint MLE for NB2 (matches MASS::glm.nb)
start = np.append(pois.params.values, 1.0)
nb2 = smf.negativebinomial("vacancies ~ C(size) + C(public) + C(nace)",
                           data=df).fit(start_params=start,
                                        method="bfgs", maxiter=500, disp=0)

5 Rootograms

We display counts up to \(k = 20\). Vacancies in the JVS are very right-skewed (≈ 80% zeros, mean ≈ 1, max in the hundreds), so 20 is enough to show what matters: zeros, the small-count region, and the beginning of the tail.

5.1 R — topmodels::rootogram

topmodels::rootogram() takes a fitted model and produces a hanging rootogram by default.

rootogram(pois, plot = TRUE, 
          main = "Poisson", 
          xlim = c(0,20))
rootogram(nb2, plot = TRUE, 
          main = "Negative binomial (NB2)",
          xlim = c(0,20))

5.2 Python — manual implementation

Same recipe as topmodels: observed counts, expected counts on the \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) scale, bars hanging from the expected curve. The expected count for value \(k\) is the sum across observations of the fitted PMF evaluated at \(k\).

For NB2, statsmodels parametrises overdispersion via \(\alpha = 1/\theta\) so \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu + \alpha\mu^2\). To map to scipy.stats.nbinom(n, p) use \(n = 1/\alpha\) and \(p = n/(n + \mu)\).

def rootogram(model, y, max_count=20, dist="poisson", ax=None,
              title=None):
    """Hanging rootogram for a fitted Poisson or NB2 GLM.

    model : statsmodels results object with .predict() returning fitted means
    y     : observed response (1d array-like of non-negative ints)
    dist  : "poisson" or "nbinom"
    """
    mu = np.asarray(model.predict())
    y  = np.asarray(y)
    ks = np.arange(max_count + 1)

    observed = np.array([(y == k).sum() for k in ks], dtype=float)

    if dist == "poisson":
        expected = np.array([poisson.pmf(k, mu).sum() for k in ks])
    elif dist == "nbinom":
        alpha = float(model.params["alpha"])
        n = 1.0 / alpha
        p = n / (n + mu)
        expected = np.array([nbinom.pmf(k, n, p).sum() for k in ks])
    else:
        raise ValueError("dist must be 'poisson' or 'nbinom'")

    obs_root = np.sqrt(observed)
    exp_root = np.sqrt(expected)

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))

    ax.bar(ks, obs_root, bottom=exp_root - obs_root, width=0.7,
           color="lightgray", edgecolor="black", label="observed")
    ax.plot(ks, exp_root, "ro-", linewidth=1.5, markersize=4,
            label=r"$\sqrt{\mathrm{expected}}$")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xlabel("count")
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$\sqrt{\mathrm{frequency}}$")
    ax.set_xticks(ks[::2])
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend(loc="upper right")
    return ax
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
rootogram(pois, df["vacancies"], dist="poisson", ax=ax, title="Poisson")
plt.show()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
rootogram(nb2, df["vacancies"], dist="nbinom", ax=ax,
          title="Negative binomial (NB2)")
plt.show()

6 Numerical comparison

The picture is also visible in the raw observed/expected counts.

  • R
  • Python
ks <- 0:10
obs <- as.numeric(table(factor(df$vacancies, levels = ks)))

mu_p <- predict(pois, type = "response")
exp_p <- sapply(ks, function(k) sum(dpois(k, lambda = mu_p)))

mu_n  <- predict(nb2, type = "response")
theta <- nb2$theta
exp_n <- sapply(ks, function(k) sum(dnbinom(k, mu = mu_n, size = theta)))

round(data.frame(k = ks,
                 observed   = obs,
                 exp_pois   = exp_p,
                 exp_nb2    = exp_n,
                 diff_pois  = obs - exp_p,
                 diff_nb2   = obs - exp_n), 1)

obs = np.array([(df["vacancies"] == k).sum() for k in ks], dtype=float)

mu_p  = pois.predict()
exp_p = np.array([poisson.pmf(k, mu_p).sum() for k in ks])

alpha = float(nb2.params["alpha"])

7 What the rootograms tell us

Both models have the same mean structure (Poisson QMLE and NB2 give nearly identical \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\), see notebook 09a), but they imply different distributions:

  • Poisson badly under-predicts the zeros (bars dip well below the line at \(k = 0\)) and over-predicts the small positive counts (\(k = 1, 2, 3\)). This is the signature of overdispersion: the Poisson variance \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu\) is too small, so mass gets concentrated near \(\mu\) instead of being spread over zeros and the long tail.
  • NB2 has \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta\). The extra variance lets it match the zeros and the right tail. Bar bottoms sit much closer to the zero line.

Conclusion (consistent with notebook 09a): use NB2 (or another distribution with extra variance) when you need the distribution of \(Y\) — for example to predict the proportion of firms with zero vacancies, or to simulate from the fitted model. For the mean \(E(Y \mid X)\) alone, Poisson with robust standard errors is enough.
